analysis.one_liner: Caps interest on loans backed by federal and military pensions and lets retirees sue lenders who take their benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in any of the four committees it was sent to; it died when the 115th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The ASSURE Act targeted companies that give retirees and veterans cash up front in exchange for part of their federal or military pension payments. It would have treated those deals like loans, capped the implied interest rate at the Federal funds rate plus 6%, required clear disclosures, and let retirees who were signed into a prohibited pension assignment sue for triple their damages plus attorney's fees. It was introduced in the final weeks of the 115th Congress, referred to four House committees, and never taken up by any of them.
analysis.who_benefits: Military retirees, veterans receiving disability or survivor benefits, and federal civil-service retirees who are offered lump-sum cash deals or loans secured by their pension payments. These products often carry effective costs far above normal loan rates, and current law generally bars assigning these benefits but is hard for an individual to enforce.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules treating any payment that diminishes a retiree's control over their federal or military pension as an extension of credit, triggering standard loan disclosures, and caps the interest rate on such credit at the Federal funds rate plus 6%.

Requires extra disclosures from anyone selling a pension-related financial product, including telling consumers whether an insured bank also offers the product, and directs the CFPB to study products that target military and federal retirees and report to Congress within three months.

Creates a private right of action letting veterans, military retirees, and federal pension recipients sue anyone who acquired their benefits in violation of the assignment prohibitions, recovering triple damages plus court costs and attorney's fees.

Clarifies that any arrangement giving another person the right to a retiree's payments for consideration is a void assignment, closing the gap between companies structured as 'purchase' deals rather than loans.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that advance cash against or buy streams of federal and military pension payments, and consumer lenders who use pension income as the basis for high-rate credit. They would face a near-binding rate cap, new disclosure rules, and treble-damages lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The interest cap (Federal funds rate plus 6%) is so low that it would effectively shut down the pension-advance market rather than regulate it, including deals some retirees enter willingly when they need cash before their pension arrives; those retirees would lose that option entirely.
Retirees with poor credit who rely on their pension as their main asset could lose access to any credit secured by it, since lenders would be unable to charge a rate that reflects the risk.

Treble damages plus mandatory attorney's fees would invite litigation against a wide range of financial arrangements touching pensions, and the bill defines covered arrangements broadly enough that legitimate transactions could get swept in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the retirees these products target, the bill offered strong protection: pension-advance deals routinely carry effective annual costs in the double or triple digits against a benefit stream that federal law already says cannot be assigned. The trade-off is real but narrow — a retiree who understood the terms and still wanted a lump sum would lose that option, and lenders would exit the market rather than lend at the capped rate. On balance, the protections outweigh the lost access for the affected population, though the cap is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the 115th Congress and referred to four House committees; none of them scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on December 13, 2018, less than three weeks before the 115th Congress expired.

It was referred to the Financial Services, Veterans' Affairs, Armed Services, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees, and to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel the next day.
No committee took further action: the bill's action history shows no hearings, markups, votes, or floor consideration.
The bill had no cosponsors at any point.

The bill would have capped interest on credit backed by federal and military pensions at the Federal funds rate plus 6%, required CFPB disclosures for pension-related products, and created a triple-damages private right of action for prohibited pension assignments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pension-advance and pension-factoring companies are better off — the rate cap, disclosures, and treble-damages lawsuits they would have faced never took effect, and retirees remained exposed to the products the bill targeted.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; no other member cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other member took a public position, so no partisan pattern can be measured; the bill was a single Democratic sponsor's measure in a Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: These firms give retirees cash in exchange for future pension payments, structures the bill would have deemed void assignments subject to triple damages, and loans against pensions would have been capped near zero interest. Their business model depends on charging retirees far more than the cash they hand over.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders using pension income to underwrite credit
industries.note: Any lender that considers a federal or military pension in deciding ability to repay would have faced the rate cap and added disclosure rules, removing their ability to price these loans at high rates.
The bill would have required pension-product sellers to disclose whether an insured bank offers a comparable product, which could steer business toward banks offering cheaper alternatives.
